previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a complex medical history including chronic diastolic heart failure, type II diabetes, chronic kidney disease, alcoholic cirrhosis, and Crohn’s disease was admitted for severe hyponatremia (Na 118) detected in cardiology clinic. The hyponatremia was attributed to over-diuresis from metolazone, leading to hypovolemic hyponatremia. She was managed in the ICU with cautious IV normal saline, resulting in gradual correction to 131 at discharge. During admission, she also had a mild respiratory illness with cough and green sputum; imaging showed atelectasis, and though sputum initially grew MRSA, it was deemed colonization, and antibiotics were discontinued. Her acute kidney injury (creatinine up to 2.7) improved with hydration to baseline (1.5). Flank pain was attributed to lumbosacral disc disease rather than renal causes. Metolazone, felodipine, and omeprazole were discontinued. She was discharged home with services, stable on adjusted medications including reduced-dose torsemide, with follow-up planned for labs and cardiology.
